claim: Mumbai was once seven separate islands: the Gazetteer of Bombay City and Island (1909) says Bombay consisted of seven separate islands, little changed until the eighteenth century; MCGM's own city profile says the city was once made up of seven small islands.

evidence.quote: originally consisted of seven separate islands

evidence.locator: City Profile of Greater Mumbai, 1.1.1 Physical Description (mcgm_city_profile.txt line ~10)
evidence.quote: once made up of seven small

claim: The 1909 Gazetteer's account (Edwardes) names the islands as Colaba and Old Woman's Island in the south, the main Bombay island, Mazagon, Parel, Varli (Worli) and Mahim; MCGM's profile lists Colaba and Little Colaba, Bombay Island, Mazagon, Parel, Worli and Mahim. Lists differ in the name of the Old Woman's/Little Colaba island only.

evidence.quote: Mozagaon and Parel which were located on the eastern strip
Worli on its western strip and Mahim

note: The Gazetteer's own footnote cites Govind Narayen (1863) with a different list (Mahim, Bombay, Colaba, Mahalakshmi, Varli, Mazagon, Sion): see conflicts.md K1. Say 'seven islands', name at most Colaba, Mazagon, Parel, Worli, Mahim, Bombay.

claim: The Hornby Vellard, the embankment that shut the sea out of the low central flats, was built under Governor William Hornby between 1771 and 1784 (Gazetteer; the work itself ran 1782-84 by MCGM's profile); Hornby handed over charge on 1 January 1784.
note: Window 1771-84 is Hornby's governorship; MCGM gives start 1782 citing Duff 1921. Say 'finished in 1784'.

claim: Before the Vellard the sea at high tide almost divided the island in two and made the roads impassable (Grose, who visited in 1772, quoted in the 1909 Gazetteer).
note: Quoting Grose, an eyewitness; Gazetteer author Edwardes compiled for the Government of Bombay.

claim: Hornby is said to have started the Vellard without the Court of Directors' sanction, with 18 months left of his term; the Gazetteer prints this as an anecdote from Maclean's Guide to Bombay, and MCGM's profile says the plan was rejected by the Directors.

evidence.quote: rejection of the plan from the Directors

note: HEDGE: the Gazetteer calls it 'an amusing anecdote'. Say 'reportedly' or 'the Company's Directors had refused'.

claim: The last island to be joined was Colaba, by the Colaba Causeway in 1838; the Gazetteer calls Colaba until then 'the only remaining vestige of the original seven islands'.

evidence.quote: the only remaining vestige of the original seven islands
Colaba island was joined with Bombay in 1838

claim: In 1909 the island (peninsula) of Bombay, which includes Colaba, covered 22.48 square miles (58.2 km2); MCGM's profile puts today's Island City at 67.79 km2 (its Table 1 says 68.71), about 16-18% more. The two figures use different definitions, so the difference is only indicative.
The causeway from Mahim to Bandra (Salsette) opened in 1845 (Gazetteer) / was completed in 1845 (MCGM). It joins the island group to Salsette; it is not one of the seven.
Sion Causeway: commenced 1798, completed 1803 (Gazetteer); MCGM's profile says 1802.
note: See conflicts.md K2. Do not use a Sion date.
